Big Brother star and glamour model Casey Batchelor has fully unveiled her first clothing range with Honeyz.com, a summer collection of boho frocks, paisley prints, and maxi dresses inspired by the seventies trends seen on the SS15 catwalks. She models the pieces herself and designed matching accessories, calling the launch a "dream come true." Casey also said her recent breast reduction has let her experiment with different styles and wear clothes more comfortably.

Candlestick Park, the San Francisco sports venue completed in 1960 and home to the Giants and later the 49ers, has been demolished to make way for houses, a hotel and a shopping center. The 49ers played there for 43 seasons, with Joe Montana leading them to four Super Bowl wins, and the stadium hosted eight NFC Championship games and two World Series (1962 and 1989). The 1989 World Series is remembered for a massive earthquake that struck during Game 3.

Wellness entrepreneur Belle Gibson, founder of The Whole Pantry app, admitted in an Australian Women's Weekly interview that her terminal brain cancer diagnosis was made up, saying "none of it's true" and asking former fans to see her as "human." Psychologist Jo Lamble, who has not treated Gibson, told Daily Mail Australia that her lack of remorse and pursuit of fame, fortune, and book deals suggest narcissism and anti-social personality disorder, rather than Munchausen Syndrome, which typically involves self-harm and seeking attention rather than money.

Manchester United's 3-0 defeat at Everton, a performance the writer calls horrendous, showed they still have a long way to go to challenge for domestic and European glory, and that they look far more beatable without Michael Carrick. Daley Blind is described as a slower, weaker version of Carrick, so the writer argues United need reinforcements. He suggests raiding Borussia Dortmund for Ilkay Gundogan, Sven Bender (the "German Carrick") and playmaker Henrikh Mkhitaryan.

In Yakutsk, eastern Russia, a baiting competition ties a five-year-old bear named Masha to a tree by her neck while dogs are released to find her, bark menacingly, and bite her, with higher scores awarded for fiercer harassment and more bites. The event, held at the Bayanay Hunting Club in the Sakha Republic, is meant to hone hunting skills and crown the best bear-hunting dog, and is viewed as a mainstream activity in Russia, where bears pose a danger to people. The images are likely to anger animal rights groups in the West, while the dog owners say Masha has been used in the

Rabie Dardouna, a 33-year-old Palestinian man, says he was duped into selling a Banksy mural for about £100 without knowing its value. The artwork, "Bomb Damage," was painted on the metal door of his family's destroyed Gaza home, and he now wants it back. The buyer, local artist Belal Khaled, says he bought it only to protect and preserve the painting, has no financial motive, and hopes to show it in Gaza exhibits, while the dispute has sparked debate on Facebook.

Photographers across the UK captured striking images of the Lyrid meteor shower overnight, with the annual event peaking at between ten and 20 meteors an hour. One photographer, Nick Watson, even caught the Northern Lights in his shot over Lindisfarne Castle in Northumberland. The shower, observed for 2,700 years and best seen from Europe, continues into Saturday, so viewers who missed the peak still have a chance to spot some meteors.

Farmer Bruce Cook of Lake Charm, Victoria, built a hay bale sculpture depicting a bull and cow mating, which police say could bring charges of "publishing pornographic images" after a complaint about its offensive nature. Cook, who erected the piece on Good Friday as "a bit of fun," has refused to remove it without a court order, saying passersby have enjoyed it and stopped to take photos. He plans to add fairy lights and two calves to the sculpture.

Two models, Maria Sidorova and Lidia Fetisova, posed seductively with Stephen, an 18-year-old, 650kg brown bear, in a forest outside Moscow for an anti-hunting campaign meant to promote living "side-by-side" with bears. The campaign's message was undercut when one model was photographed wearing a fur coat, though it's unclear whether the fur was real. Stephen was rescued as a cub from hunters by his owner, Yuriy Panteleenko, a circus trainer who hand-raised him after he proved unable to return to the wild.

Lawyers for the parents of Michael Brown, the unarmed 18-year-old fatally shot by white Ferguson police officer Darren Wilson in August 2014, announced they would file a wrongful death lawsuit against the city of Ferguson the following day. Attorneys previously said the suit would also name Wilson, who resigned in November after neither a grand jury nor the Justice Department prosecuted him. A Justice Department report later cited racial bias in Ferguson's police department and court system, leading to several city officials' resignations.

Zoo Weekly drew widespread condemnation from social media users and the Department of Veteran Affairs over its "Special Anzac Centenary Issue," which featured a half-naked model holding a poppy. The DVA noted that the word "Anzac" is federally protected and cannot be used commercially without ministerial permission, and it asked Zoo to remove all offending images, which the magazine did from Facebook. The controversy came alongside criticism of Woolworths for its "Fresh in our Memories" Anzac campaign, which the supermarket has since been forced to halt.

The article looks at how travel could change over the coming decades, predicting that by 2030 digital advances will make booking and planning trips as easy as buying a book on Amazon, with personalised suggestions from predictive software and possibly an "e-agent" worn as a watch or jewellery. It also forecasts that airport check-in lines and desks will disappear, replaced by automated bag drops, biometric face recognition, digital boarding passes, and high-speed laser scanners that clear customs and security in seconds.

The BBC was accused of a left-wing stitch-up after David Cameron was repeatedly interrupted during a Radio 1 interview, in which host Chris Smith offered to bet him £1,000 that he wouldn't win a majority. Listeners on Twitter called the interview 'appalling' and the host 'hostile,' 'childish' and 'arrogant.' The Prime Minister was also pressed on ruling out a deal with the DUP and clashed with an audience member over his stance on Mediterranean migrants.

A lone lioness in Zimbabwe's Hwange National Park single-handedly brought down a giraffe after the rest of her pride abandoned the hunt to chase an easier target, a passing warthog. Researcher Brent Stapelkamp, who witnessed the struggle, said she bit the giraffe's chest to make it fall before locking onto its throat for the kill, despite the danger of its deadly kicks. Her determination was later explained when Stapelkamp noticed she had been nursing, indicating she had newly born cubs hidden away waiting to be fed.

Police and emergency crews are continuing a large-scale search through thick bushland near Lake Eildon, Victoria, for 11-year-old autistic boy Luke Shambrook, who went missing from a campsite on Good Friday. A family reported seeing a boy matching his description near Devils River, four kilometres from the campsite, and police remain hopeful he is alive, noting his high pain tolerance and that he was last seen wearing a beanie and warm jacket. Luke has limited speech and may not realise he is lost, while overnight temperatures dropping to around eight degrees add urgency to the search on its fourth day.

The article describes a troubling trend in which girls as young as ten or eleven record "hot or not" videos on webcams, publicly rating classmates' looks before posting them to YouTube, where one clip drew 120 views within days. It warns that this online cruelty leaves its targets humiliated and in tears, and it ties the phenomenon to a culture in which young girls grow up fast and worry about their appearance, with half of three-to-six-year-olds saying they fear being fat.

Supermodel Kate Upton, 22, maintains her figure through a strict diet and exercise regime, following an "ABC rule" of no alcohol, bread or processed carbohydrates, plus a 48-hour juice cleanse before big shoots or film scenes. She eats lean, green meals such as eggs on spinach, grilled chicken with quinoa, and kale salad, avoids red meat, eats only certain fruits, and allows herself the occasional "cheat day" of salty fried food. Upton told the Evening Standard her goal is being strong enough to work ten-hour days while eating healthily.

David Tungate, 58, is engaged to a third Gambian woman after his first marriage ended in divorce and his second wife, a serial bigamist, conned him out of £24,000 of his retirement money, leaving him close to bankruptcy. Undeterred by the experiences, he admits he may seem gullible but says he always follows his heart and feels blessed with his new fiancée. His troubles began after a 1998 holiday in Gambia, where he married Nyima Sye and brought her to the UK, though they divorced five years later. Years afterward he met Ndey, a waitress, and began sending her money to help her.

Chancellor George Osborne warned that Labour would raise taxes again, citing figures showing taxes on earnings rose by nearly £1,900 under 13 years of Labour, and said Ed Miliband and Ed Balls "would do it all over again." David Cameron, beginning a tour of the UK's four nations, said voters have one month to avoid a Miliband government, claiming Labour would pull nearly a million more people into the 40p tax rate, while Ed Balls countered that the Tories would make "millions pay more while millionaires pay less." Meanwhile, a spat erupted between the Tories and Lib

Sarah Weatherill, a 31-year-old mother-of-four and law student from Coventry, became addicted to Red Bull in 2009 and was drinking up to 24 cans a day at a cost of about £5,460 a year. The habit left her lethargic, depressed, anxious and suffering heart palpitations, and she had to cut down to eight cans daily beforehand because stopping abruptly could have caused a seizure. She claims a single 50-minute hypnotherapy session earlier this month cured her of the addiction.

Severe weather, including thunderstorms, tornadoes, hail, and strong winds, is forecast to hit multiple states from Friday through Sunday, affecting cities such as Dallas, Houston, Oklahoma City, Nashville, Atlanta, and New Orleans, with flash flooding possible on Monday. The forecast follows a harmless tornado near Belle Glade, Florida, and two tornadoes in Colorado on Thursday. Meanwhile, snow fell in parts of the country, including during a Yankees-Tigers baseball game on Wednesday.

Paul Nungesser, a German student accused of rape by classmate Emma Sulkowicz, has sued Columbia University, alleging gender-based harassment and defamation. He claims the school failed to protect him after authorities rejected Sulkowicz's allegations, by presenting them as fact on a university website and letting her carry a mattress around campus as an approved senior art thesis, which he says created a hostile environment and has hurt his job prospects. The suit, filed in Manhattan federal court against the school, its trustees, President Lee Bollinger, and Professor Jon Kessler, seeks unspecified damages;

North Dakota Republican Rep. Randy Boehning, who has voted against gay rights for over a decade, was outed as a user of the gay hook-up app Grindr after a 21-year-old Bismarck man, Dustin Smith, recognized him and took explicit messages and a photo Boehning had sent him to the press. Boehning acknowledged being gay and using the app, but claimed he was targeted in retaliation for voting against an anti-discrimination bill, though he has refused to name the lawmaker he says made the threat.

According to eyewitnesses quoted in the Daily Mail, Oscar winner Octavia Spencer behaved rudely at a Barnes & Noble book signing in Los Angeles for her children's book "Randi Rhodes Ninja Detective — The Sweetest Heist in History." Fan Angel Guzman said she gave short, blunt answers during the Q&A, complained about the space and her water, took a long bathroom break, and refused to engage with fans or pose for photos. Some attendees reportedly pulled their kids out of line, demanded refunds, and left the store.

Earlier this month, Canadian meteorologist Kristi Gordon received hate mail criticizing her appearance while six months pregnant, and she read excerpts on air to a wave of public support. Australian presenter Nicky Buckley, who faced similar abuse in 1997 for appearing on "The Sale of the Century" in figure-hugging gowns while pregnant, describes the backlash in her new memoir. Buckley says critics jammed fax machines at Channel 9 and newspapers, but she kept working because she had a mortgage and a right to do her job.

Geraldine Alcorn, a 29-year-old former Pittsburgh elementary school teacher accused of an obsessive attachment to an 11-year-old student, waived a preliminary hearing on a felony charge of interfering with the girl's custody. In exchange, prosecutors dropped two misdemeanor charges (luring a child into a vehicle and corruption of minors), so she must now stand trial or seek a plea deal.

Prosecutors allege she hid her phone number on the girl's math homework, exchanged thousands of texts with her, and spoke of adopting her and running away together before resigning in March. The gir

Paige VanZant, 21, and Felice Herrig had to be pulled apart during their staredown ahead of their strawweight fight in New Jersey on Saturday. VanZant, who has just five pro fights and an individual Reebok contract, is being hyped as the UFC's next big thing, while Herrig said she's the better striker, grappler, and athlete and that beating the hyped VanZant would make her victory sweeter. VanZant, who made her UFC debut with a third-round stoppage of Kailin Curran last November, called being part of the UFC surreal and said she accepted the fight right away.

Hotel owner Jon Huxley, 46, plans to convert his Westward Ho! hotel in Folkestone, Kent, into a venue for the swinging and gay communities, with sex swings, bondage rooms, and dungeons, hoping to capitalise on the Fifty Shades of Grey craze. He turned to this idea after a dispute with Shepway District Council, which issued an enforcement notice over the Grade-II listed building's use as housing for homeless people following neighbours' complaints of anti-social behaviour. Huxley says the business will be a "civilised and friendly" all-inclusive environment with

Ravi Beefnah, 34, covered his £35,000 Audi A5 with slogans and has parked it outside the Chelmsford, Essex dealership where he bought it for two months, claiming the car uses about a litre of oil every 250 miles and that Audi has failed to resolve his complaint. He says the fault in the 2011 TFSI petrol engine is widespread, and he is taking the dealership to court and demanding £9,000 for repairs. Audi admits some engines had a problem and has offered to fix affected cars free of charge, but Beefnah says he will leave the car there until his civil case is resolved.

Astronomer Dr William Hartmann suggests that the bright light that led Paul the Apostle to convert to Christianity near Damascus around the 30s C.E. may have been a meteor. He argues in the journal Meteoritics and Planetary Science that the Bible's three accounts of Paul's experience, including his three days of blindness, closely match a Chelyabinsk-class or Tunguska-class fireball. The article compares this to the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor in Russia, which injured more than 1,600 people.

The Fire Brigades Union warns that overstretched ambulance services are increasingly sending firemen, many without basic first aid training, to 999 emergencies, leaving seriously ill patients waiting up to hours for paramedics. The union calls the practice irresponsible and dangerous, citing cases such as an elderly woman feared to have died after nearly 40 minutes in firefighters' care. Ambulance services face unprecedented demand from an ageing population, rising non-urgent calls, and delays handing patients over at busy A&E units.

Six hostages who hid in a supermarket freezer during the January attacks at the Hyper Cacher Jewish store in Paris have sued French media for broadcasting their location live during the siege. Their lawyer, Patrick Klugman, says outlets like BFMTV lacked basic precautions and could have endangered the group, which included a three-year-old and a one-month-old baby, especially since gunman Amedy Coulibaly was following the coverage and had been in contact with BFMTV journalists. The suit accuses the media of endangering lives by ignoring security protocols, an offense carrying a maximum penalty of a year

The Salt card is a credit card-sized gadget that connects via Bluetooth to an app on an Android phone or iPhone, automatically unlocking the device when the user is nearby and locking it again once they move about 10 feet away. Created by Chicago-based Joel Paglione and Niko Zistakis, it is meant to save users roughly 53 hours a year and is claimed to be more secure than fingerprint scanners. The card also alerts users if they stray too far from their wallet, and the duo raised over $82,000 on Kickstarter to put it into production.

Ryan Heritage, an 18-year-old from Wiltshire wanted for alleged fraud and theft, taunted Trowbridge police on their Facebook page, daring them to check for a warrant and catch him. Hours later, police spotted him on a night out, chased him on foot, and arrested him, then reposted his message with the comment "His luck ran out #arrested." He was charged with theft, burglary, and failing to answer bail on fraud charges, and was bailed to appear in court in June and May.

Detectives investigating the suspected murder of landlady Deborah Steel, who vanished from her Ely pub, the Royal Standard, in December 1997, dug up the pub's patio but found no clues. Her body has never been found, and police recently reclassified the case as a murder inquiry. A 73-year-old man remains on bail, and her sister says the unsolved case has been a heavy burden for the family.

Nicole McDonough, a 32-year-old New Jersey high school teacher indicted for allegedly having sex with one 18-year-old student and engaging in improper communication and fraternization with two others, has applied for Morris County's Pre-Trial Intervention program. If accepted and she completes the one-to-three-year probationary program, the charges would be dropped and her record expunged. A prosecutor argues she is likely ineligible because of the three charges, and a judge will decide after hearing arguments from both sides.

William Hilton Paul, 22, son of Republican presidential candidate Rand Paul, was cited for a DUI after crashing his truck into an unoccupied parked car in Lexington, Kentucky. He failed a field sobriety test and refused blood and breathalyzer tests, but was not arrested because police protocol applies when a DUI suspect is hospitalized. This is his third alcohol-related run-in with the law, and he is scheduled to be arraigned on May 12, while the senator's campaign declined to comment on the private family matter.

Kerrie Armitage, a 28-year-old mother of three from Leeds, has aquagenic urticaria, an ultra-rare allergy to water that she was diagnosed with two years ago after her skin blistered in a rain storm. The saliva on her husband Peter's lips can trigger painful hives, so he must dry his lips before kissing her, and even hugging her children can set off a reaction because their body heat makes her sweat. The condition affects her daily life, forcing her to give up her job as a cleaner and choose between tasks like washing up and bathing her kids.

Christien Sechrist, a 20-year-old from Houston, Texas, got a large black-and-white tattoo of his toddler son Perseus's portrait on the left side of his face in July, as a tribute to the boy he almost lost. A photo of the tattoo recently went viral on Imgur, drawing criticism from friends who questioned its visible placement and warned it could hurt his job prospects. Christien says he doesn't regret the tattoo and would happily get it again.

Real Madrid have until Thursday, April 30 to decide whether to use their exclusive option to buy Manchester United loanee Javier Hernandez, after which United will be free to consider offers of around £10million from West Ham, Southampton and Lazio. Coach Carlo Ancelotti said the club would evaluate the situation at the end of the season, praising the striker's professionalism. Hernandez has scored three goals in his last two games, boosting his valuation, and has one year left on his Old Trafford contract.

Google marked the 81st anniversary of the 1934 "Surgeon's Photograph," the Daily Mail image that claimed to show a monster in Loch Ness, by launching a Street View experience that lets users explore the Scottish loch both above and beneath the water. It also released a commemorative Google Doodle and swapped the yellow Pegman for a Nessie peg-monster. The imagery was captured in partnership with Catlin Seaview Survey and Adrian Shine of the Loch Ness and Morar Project, and Google noted the photo is the loch's most iconic image and possibly one of the most elaborate

Police arrested Alyssa Chang this week for allegedly helping the child's 65-year-old grandmother abduct 2-year-old Ronnie Tran, after the two women reportedly bound the boy's mother with plastic ties, took her and the child to another home, and left her locked in a cupboard. Chang's brother, John Truong, unknowingly babysat the toddler that night, believing the boy was her boyfriend's son, and called police after seeing the Amber Alert online the next morning. The boy was found safe and unhurt, and Truong said he was stunned by his sister's arrest.

A radio poll found more than 70 per cent of voters believe Manchester United will win the title next season, prompting the author to ask whether that is fan optimism or real faith in Louis van Gaal, a proven winner who is rebuilding the club after David Moyes. The author argues Van Gaal will be judged against Sir Alex Ferguson's legacy, that both underachieved in Europe, and that United should be challenging for the title next season but still need to improve to compete for both the Premier League and the Champions League.

Spain's Ciudad Real airport, built in 2009 at a cost of over €1 billion to relieve Madrid's Barajas airport, closed in 2012 after its parent company ran into financial trouble. A judge ordered it sold with a €100 million asking price, but with no buyers, there is now no minimum price, so it could go for as little as £1. Whoever buys it would also have to take on a few hundred million pounds of debt.

Researchers at the University of Bath and Yale University say they have developed a new patented molecular catalyst that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen more efficiently than any existing material, with energy loss that is "almost non-existent." This could make hydrogen production less dependent on fossil fuels and let hydrogen serve as a way to store energy from renewable sources like wind and solar, which is difficult to do with batteries alone.

Police confirmed that the body found in the boot of a car in Bermagui, NSW, on Wednesday night is that of 35-year-old Canberra public servant Daniela D'Addario. Her 27-year-old boyfriend, Josaia "Joey" Vosikata, fled from officers into bushland, was arrested the next day, and has been extradited to the ACT and charged with her murder. Friends described their four-month relationship as tumultuous, saying she had discovered a month earlier that he had a wife and children in Fiji.

A video filmed in Pennsylvania shows Sam, a five-year-old German Shepherd, struggling to stay awake while watching TV on the couch. His head repeatedly dips and he startles himself awake before finally yawning, rolling over, and snuggling up to his owner. The clip, which has smooth jazz dubbed over it, has been watched more than 100,000 times, with viewers calling it "cute" and "adorable."

EU leaders agreed at an emergency summit to send warships and triple funding for Mediterranean rescue patrols after some 1,700 migrants died in the past week, with Britain's HMS Bulwark and Germany's Berlin expected to deploy within days. Italian PM Matteo Renzi called the package "a giant step forward," while Malta's PM Joseph Muscat warned the proposed assets would "never be enough." Meanwhile, victims of the worst-ever Mediterranean migrant disaster were buried in Malta, and David Cameron stressed Britain would not take in more migrants.

Islamic State has reportedly launched its own health service, the "Islamic State Health Service" (ISHS), whose name and promotional imagery closely resemble those of the UK's National Health Service. A video released on social media features an Australian pediatrician, known as Abu Yusuf al-Australi, and an Indian physiologist urging foreign doctors to travel to Syria to help with the new service. The footage shows the Australian doctor treating babies in a maternity unit and training other doctors, while he says Muslim medical professionals in the West should have come sooner because the region lacks qualified staff.

The author argues that Arsenal fans who call Chelsea boring for defending well overlook their own side's grinding 2003-04 unbeaten run, and should instead focus on their players' shortcomings, particularly Mesut Ozil. Despite recent sublime form, Ozil was merely tidy in Sunday's match against Chelsea, failed to influence the result, and missed a gaping goal. The author concludes that he did not show he is world class or worth his £42m fee, and that Cesc Fabregas outshone him.

A staff member in Rep. Mike Doyle's Washington office opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Wednesday, prompting a temporary quarantine of Room 239 in the Cannon House Office Building while hazmat teams tested it. The tests came back negative, the area reopened after under two hours, and the staffer was told only to wash her hands. The substance and its sender remain unidentified, and an investigation is ongoing.

Housekeeper Kim Roberts, 58, admitted stealing antiques and art worth around £500,000 – including a Picasso sketch, vases, pewter plates and silverware – from the 87-year-old Dowager Countess Bathurst's Cirencester mansion and London home, and was warned at Gloucester Crown Court that she faces a lengthy jail term. Roberts also admitted burgling the countess's Kensington home, stealing a £45,000 Volvo XC90 from a previous employer, and committing fraud by lying about her birth year to a recruitment agency. She had earlier claimed the items were

California's parole board granted parole to 63-year-old James Schoenfeld on the 20th time it considered his case, 39 years after he and two accomplices kidnapped 26 schoolchildren and their bus driver in 1976. The kidnappers, inspired by the film *Dirty Harry*, buried their victims alive in an underground trailer while demanding a $5 million ransom. The ruling will undergo an internal review of up to four months before a recommended parole date goes to Governor Jerry Brown.

The Great Dying, which occurred 252 million years ago, wiped out more than 96% of the world's creatures. A University of Edinburgh-led study is the first to show that highly acidic oceans were the main cause of death, as huge volcanic eruptions released carbon dioxide that was absorbed by the seas and changed their chemistry. Researchers said the amount of carbon added to the atmosphere was "probably greater than today's fossil fuel reserves," and the extinction unfolded over 60,000 years, with ocean acidification lasting around 10,000 years.

Jennifer Drew, a 31-year-old mother-of-one from Leicestershire, has saved £17,000 over three years by spending an hour a day hunting for deals and coupons, using newspaper coupons and voucher sites like Wowcher and Groupon. Her stockpile of multi-buy bargains, including items she doesn't need and gives to friends, now fills a room and her garage, and she estimates she saves £70 a week on food, once getting a £140 shop for just 29p. Her couponing began during her pregnancy after she watched the American show Extreme Couponing, and it became more valuable when her husband was made

Canadian tourist Charlene Fritz, 35, was visiting Snow Hill Island in Antarctica during an expedition when a baby elephant seal, roughly two months old and about 200lbs, climbed onto her for a cuddle, making it hard for her to sit upright. Expedition rules forbade her from touching or approaching the pup, so the seal made all the moves, and Fritz described the moment as one she'll never forget. She later learned the pup's friendliness may have been linked to the harsh weaning process, in which mothers fatten their young for about a month and then abandon them to fend for themselves.

Xie Shisheng, now 34, was rescued this week from a cotton mill in Qingyuan, China, where he had been locked in a dark room, beaten daily, and treated like a slave since age 16. Authorities discovered him after being tipped off about an illegal mill producing fake cotton goods; he said he was hit with a hammer, force-fed, and never fed properly. Neighbours had long suspected someone was being held there, and the mill's owners fled when police arrived.

A five-year-old Chinese girl, Jiaojiao, survived a 150ft fall from a window in Zheng Du City after her mother left her home alone for 10 minutes to buy takeaway food. Rain canopies, laundry racks and wet grass broke her fall, but she suffered a punctured lung, multiple fractures, a shattered pelvis and internal bleeding. After an emergency blood transfusion and surgery, she remains in intensive care, while her mother says she cannot afford the roughly £100,000 medical bill.

SBS news reporter Ellie Laing wrote an open letter responding to an article in The Australian that suggested News and Current Affairs Director Jim Carroll was taking a more "commercial" approach by hiring young, attractive, female Anglo-Celtic journalists, a claim Carroll denies. Laing said she welcomes compliments about her looks but rejected the idea that being "attractive," white and a woman undermines the credibility of the news service. She pointed to her nearly decade of experience across the ABC, Seven and Ten, her hard work, and her teaching job, and defended SBS's inclusion of arts co

An 18-year-old New Yorker who goes by Dark.Cyanide climbs some of the city's tallest buildings without ropes or harnesses, sitting on precarious ledges to photograph dizzying views, including some taken 72 storeys up. He says security guards and strong winds at high altitude are his biggest obstacles, and that he loves photographing New York because it is huge and constantly changing, offering new vantage points as new skyscrapers rise.

Designers worldwide are developing more comfortable economy and premium economy airplane seats with extra legroom, but passengers will have to wait a few years for them to arrive. Crawley-based Acro Aircraft Seating unveiled its "Series 7" premium economy seat, which uses an aluminium chassis, composite materials, and hand-stitched leather armrests, and is designed to be thin and ergonomic rather than heavily padded, freeing up more space. The seats must pass a lengthy certification process and are not expected to fly until 2017.

Residents of Melbourne and Adelaide had a spectacular view of Saturday night's "blood moon" lunar eclipse, while wet and cloudy weather blocked the view in Sydney, Brisbane, Canberra and other cities. The event was one of the shortest total lunar eclipses in a long time, with totality lasting only about five to ten minutes, according to a Sydney Observatory astronomer. Observatory staff in Sydney still captured the eclipse with their equipment and shared images of the pink moon online.

Andy Murray beat Tomas Berdych 6-4, 6-4 in 1 hour 42 minutes to reach the Miami Open final, delivering a clinical performance that lacked the controversy of their Australian Open semi-final in January. He will face Novak Djokovic on Sunday in his first Masters-level final since winning the title two years ago, a sign that he is returning to the form of early 2013 after back surgery and coaching and team changes. His improved season also includes a Grand Slam final and a semi-final at Indian Wells.

British and Norwegian veterinarians have criticised EU organic farming rules that require fish to be treated first with homeopathic remedies, calling the directives "scientifically illiterate" and warning they could cause serious harm to animal health and welfare. The rules, which Norway is set to bring into national law, also limit organic farmers to mainstream medical treatments twice a year or the fish lose their organic certification, which the Norwegian Veterinary Association says could delay adequate treatment and prolong suffering. The British Veterinary Association echoed these concerns, saying it cannot endorse remedies with no proven efficacy.

A Formula One fan was arrested after climbing a 10-foot grandstand fence and sprinting across the start-finish straight during second practice for the Chinese Grand Prix. He then scaled the pit wall and entered the Ferrari garage, waving his ticket and shouting, "I want a car. I've got a ticket." He was handed over to authorities, and the FIA, promoters, and circuit officials are investigating the incident, which reportedly embarrassed Chinese officials and recalled a 2003 British GP track invasion.

Labour received £1.1 million in donations during the second week of the election campaign (April 6-12), more than twice the Conservatives' £492,512, with over £700,000 coming from trade unions such as Unison, USDAW and Unite. Most Tory money came from wealthy individuals, including a £170,000 gift from hedge fund co-founder Christopher Rokos, while the Lib Dems received about £50,000 and Ukip £8,000. The Conservatives said the union donations show Labour would be beholden to union demands for more spending, borrowing and higher taxes.

The biggest UK pension reforms in a century, which since Monday let over-55s withdraw all or part of their pension pots instead of buying an annuity, have been met with widespread confusion. Providers report callers as young as 23 trying to cash in their savings, and many people are unaware of the age limits or the heavy tax bills that can come from withdrawing everything at once. Experts also criticized the Treasury for pausing television ads for its Pension Wise guidance service under pre-election "purdah" rules, with only about 300 advisers available to provide the promised free half-hour sessions.

New Yorkers of all faiths and backgrounds filled Fifth Avenue near St Patrick's Cathedral on Easter Sunday for the annual Easter parade, showing off outlandish hats that ranged from bunny ears and flowers to a ship with blue sails and a diorama inspired by Mayor Bill de Blasio. Hatmaker Mary Ann Smith, who wore the ship hat and made butterfly and tropical umbrella headpieces for two friends, said her designs were about "sailing to new heights." The sunny, mild weather drew churchgoers from Cardinal Timothy

Matthew Colvin, 26, was arrested in Southaven, Mississippi, for stealing Elton John's heart-shaped glasses, valued at over $2,000, from a display case at Memphis' Rock 'n' Soul Museum during business hours. Investigators matched fingerprints from the case to Colvin, and after they called him, he told them the glasses were in a mailbox, where they were recovered. Colvin faces up to 12 years in prison, and the glasses were scheduled to return to display on Wednesday.

The 15-year-old son of Canada's Miami Consul General, Marc Wabafiyebazu, plans to plead not guilty if charged after an alleged drug deal turned into a gun battle that killed his 17-year-old brother, Jean, and another teen, Joshua Wright. Marc is due in juvenile court on April 8 and would not be protected by diplomatic immunity, while 19-year-old Anthony Rodriguez has been charged with second-degree murder and marijuana possession with intent to sell. The boys' mother, Roxanne Dube, expressed condolences to Wright's family and said the family w

A Loganair pilot saved his 30 passengers and three crew by wrestling control of his plane out of a North Sea nosedive with just seven seconds to spare. After the Saab 2000 was struck by lightning during a stormy Aberdeen-to-Shetland flight, the autopilot stayed engaged and countered his commands, sending the plane plunging at 9,500ft a minute to within 1,100ft of the ocean. The pilot sent a Mayday and regained control, and the aircraft landed safely in Aberdeen with only minor damage. An investigation found no technical faults, and pilot training now includes sim

Real Madrid manager Carlo Ancelotti says he will wait until the end of the season to decide on Javier Hernandez's future. The Manchester United loanee has scored four goals in four appearances, including a late winner against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League quarter-finals. Ancelotti praised the striker's professionalism and readiness, and Real next face Almeria as they try to close the gap on La Liga leaders Barcelona.

Scientists using a new dating technique on 11 rock samples from around the nearly complete Little Foot skeleton, found in South Africa's Sterkfontein Caves, determined that the fossil is about 3.7 million years old. The finding, published in Nature, shows that Little Foot, a female Australopithecus prometheus, lived around the same time as Australopithecus afarensis, the species of the famous Lucy fossil. The results may have important implications for understanding the evolutionary relationships among humankind's ancient relatives.

Paul Armstrong, 26, of Sunderland, lost his new IT project manager job before starting it after he was caught at the airport bringing a stun gun disguised as a torch, an extendable baton and a knuckle duster back from a Cyprus holiday. He pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm and two offensive weapons, and Newcastle Crown Court gave him an eight-month prison sentence suspended for two years, plus £2,000 costs. The judge said prison wasn't necessary because there was no suggestion he would use the weapons and he had no prior record, but warned the public about the gravity of bringing

London Mayor Boris Johnson admitted on Sky News that he hopes to be considered as a future Conservative Party leader after David Cameron, saying it would be "a wonderful thing," though he called it "highly unlikely" and noted the post would not be vacant for at least five years. Johnson, who is running to become MP for Uxbridge and South Ruislip, has been named by Cameron as a potential successor, along with Theresa May and George Osborne. Separately, Cameron acknowledged that his "calm smoothness" may give the wrong impression about how badly he wants to win the General Election, insisting he has "no end"

Kanye West, in an essay for Paper magazine's April cover story, said he is tired of celebrities being labeled as members of the Illuminati, arguing that if such a group existed it would resemble energy companies rather than Hollywood stars. He said musicians "don't run anything" and are merely "the face of brands," noting that they must even compromise their lyrics to avoid losing contracts. West also talked about wanting to raise his daughter North in a "truthful world" not based on brand and perception.

David Cameron acknowledges that public "fears and worries" about immigration remain and blames Labour for 13 years of failures such as bogus colleges, loopholes, and a welfare system that discouraged work. He says the Conservatives have capped skilled migration from outside the EU, closed over 850 bogus colleges, restricted benefits and housing access for migrants, introduced exit checks, and pushed for apprenticeships and welfare reform. He claims that two-thirds of job growth now benefits British citizens, compared with 10 percent under Labour, but admits more work is needed, especially on migration from within Europe, and that

The Borden family burial plot at Oak Grove Cemetery in Fall River, Massachusetts, where Lizzie Borden and the parents she was accused of killing are buried, was defaced with black and green paint over the weekend. The vandalism was discovered the day after Lifetime's miniseries *The Lizzie Borden Chronicles* premiered, and a historian suggested the show may have prompted it, noting that TV programs about Borden typically bring a surge of visitors. The plot has been vandalized before, and the cemetery director said he'd like to catch those responsible.

Ilha de Mana, a private 15-acre island off Brazil's Costa Verde near Paraty, can be rented from £2,500 ($3,750) a night and accommodates eight guests. The solar-powered island has a main residence and four over-water chalets with air-conditioned rooms, along with a heliport, a rock-carved freshwater swimming pool, and a private 100-ft beach. It sits in the sheltered bay of Angra dos Reis, about a 15-minute boat ride from Paraty and 40 minutes by helicopter from Rio de Janeiro.

Violent anti-immigrant protests that began two weeks ago in Durban and have spread to Johannesburg have left six people believed dead, with the latest victim, Carol Lloyd, injured and covered in blood when rocks shattered her car window. Police used rubber bullets and tear gas to disperse about 200 protesters, who say they want immigrants to leave amid high unemployment, while many foreign nationals have shut their shops and fled. The unrest flared after Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini reportedly said foreigners should leave, remarks he says were misinterpreted, and President Zuma has condem

The Duke of York made his first public appearance since a Florida judge struck lurid sex allegations against him from the public record, visiting AkzoNobel's Slough offices as part of his work with the Outward Bound Trust. A visibly relieved Andrew, who has always denied the claims made by Virginia Roberts, toured the paint firm and met privately with senior staff, whose UK managing director dismissed concerns about association with the Duke and praised the company's relationship with the trust. Roberts, who alleged she was a sex slave of Andrew's former friend Jeffrey Epstein, made the claims in submissions seeking

A couple, Josh and Vanessa Ellis, and their eight-month-old son Hudson were killed in Bonney Lake, Washington, when a 50-foot concrete barrier weighing tons fell from the Route 410 overpass, where workers were installing a sidewalk, and crushed their pickup truck. Investigators first believed only one person had died, and it took hours to extract the bodies. The article also notes broader concerns about US infrastructure, citing a former Transportation Secretary who said about 70,000 bridges are structurally deficient, and a 2013 ASCE grade of D+ for the nation's infr

Jean Sharon Abbott, 38, of Plymouth, Minnesota, lived for 30 years believing she had cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia), enduring muscle spasms, near immobility, and painful surgeries, before learning at 33 that she actually had dopa-responsive dystonia, a rare but treatable muscle disorder. Despite the life-changing misdiagnosis, she says she holds no resentment, crediting her supportive family and friends for a "fantastic childhood" and saying her experiences made her who she is today.

Julie Ronayne won £160,000 after a botched 2008 hysterectomy at Liverpool Women's Hospital left her swollen "like Michelin man" from a peritonitis infection, and her husband Edward was separately awarded £9,000 for the psychiatric injury he suffered from seeing her condition. The NHS trust is now challenging his payout at London's Appeal Court, arguing it could open the door to a flood of similar claims costing the health service millions. The trust's barrister contends that Mr Ronayne, who was visiting his wife in hospital, would have expected her to look unwell and so did not suff

US authorities suspected as early as 2009 that British trader Navinder Singh Sarao, 36, was making illicit trades. He is now accused of causing the 2010 "flash crash" and of making £26million from illegal trading over five years. Analysts are shocked that it took six years for charges to be brought, noting that the Chicago Mercantile Exchange warned Sarao in 2009 yet he allegedly continued manipulating the market, using special software from his London home, well into this year.

The Mail is seeking nominations for its first Mumpreneur Of The Year Award, and today's nominee is Petra Wetzel, a 40-year-old single mother from Glasgow who founded the WEST brewery in 2006 when her son Noah was a baby. Her company now turns over nearly £10 million a year, with its St Mungo lager sold in 100 Waitrose branches and some Tesco stores in Scotland, and she plans to open a second brewery later this year. Despite her success, Petra says she puts her role as a mother first, even turning down a lucrative meeting with an Italian importer because it clashed

The Kennel Club warns that more than 10,000 dogs a year are poisoned by everyday items like painkillers, chocolate, raisins, onions, and chewing gum, with about 56,000 treated between 2010 and 2014 and 470 dying. Owners often unknowingly feed dogs harmful human foods or leave dangerous items within reach, and e-cigarette refill poisonings rose 300 per cent in 2014. The charity urges owners to contact a vet immediately if they suspect poisoning, even if the dog seems well, since symptoms can take days to appear.

SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon admitted she understands English voters' concerns about her party's involvement in a coalition government, and suggested David Cameron's attacks have been "not unhelpful" because they've boosted the SNP's publicity. She also insisted she would put Ed Miliband into Downing Street even if Labour wins up to 40 fewer seats than the Tories in a hung Parliament, provided there is an anti-Tory majority. With polls suggesting the SNP could win as many as 50 of Scotland's 59 seats and hold the balance of power, Labour has ruled out a formal coalition but

Chancellor George Osborne claimed that every family would be £350 worse off if the SNP held the balance of power in a Labour government, warning of a "dangerous cocktail" of higher taxes, spending and interest rates, as well as a "constitutional crisis." His argument was based on Treasury analysis suggesting that Nicola Sturgeon's demands, including an end to austerity and the abolition of Trident, would add £6billion to Britain's interest bill. Osborne also cited warnings from global investors and banks that an SNP-Labour deal would push up mortgage rates and make it harder for businesses to expand.

England and Gloucester No 8 Ben Morgan is recovering well from a broken left leg suffered against Saracens in January, and he recently had final surgery to remove a pin from the leg. The 26-year-old, who last played for England five months ago when he scored two tries against Australia, remains part of Stuart Lancaster's World Cup plans and appears on course to feature in the warm-up period before the tournament begins in mid-September. Morgan says he is staying positive, taking recovery day by day, and believes other players will also have limited game time heading into the warm-up matches.

A new study from researchers at Caltech, George Washington University, and the University of Washington found that 15.7 percent of NFL players declare bankruptcy within 12 years of retiring, a rate of about 1.1 percent per year that matches the general U.S. population regardless of career length or earnings. The figure is far lower than a widely cited 2009 Sports Illustrated statistic claiming 78 percent of retired players face bankruptcy or financial stress within two years. High-profile examples like Warren Sapp, Michael Vick, and Vince Young went broke despite earning tens of millions, often due to extravagant spending,

Tory employment minister Esther McVey, who holds the marginal Wirral West seat with a majority of just 2,436, has called on Ed Miliband to condemn what she calls a "scurrilous" and "misogynistic and sexist" campaign against her. She has been branded "murderer McVey" in graffiti and targeted by a "Sack Esther McVey" campaign and a song claiming she is going to hell. McVey says the attacks will not intimidate her and that they show what Labour really thinks of women.

Robert Bates, a 73-year-old Tulsa reserve deputy, pleaded not guilty to second-degree manslaughter for fatally shooting Eric Harris on April 2 after, he says, mistakenly drawing his gun instead of his Taser during a botched sting. A 2009 internal sheriff's office investigation had found Bates received special treatment in training and raised concerns about his behavior in the field, such as using his personal car on duty and making unauthorized stops. Harris's attorney argues that Harris might still be alive had those findings been acted on, while the sheriff's office says no further action was taken and S

A 34-year-old cold case was solved when a Craigslist ad posted by Carol Cole's sister and a Facebook page created by Bossier Parish detectives for the unidentified "Bossier Doe" led to a connection between the two. Cole, a 17-year-old Michigan teen who escaped a Texas juvenile detention center in October 1980, was found stabbed nine times in the Louisiana woods in January 1981, and DNA confirmed her identity in February. The renewed attention has also produced a person of interest, John Chesson, who is already in prison for an unrelated murder.

Anti-racism protester Jacob King of Melbourne was photographed face-to-face with a bald man with a swastika tattoo at the Easter weekend Reclaim Australia rally at Federation Square. King said he spread his arms to protect fellow protesters, expecting an attack, but felt unexpected compassion because he had once held Islamophobic views himself. He told the man there would be no more fighting, and was surprised and respectful when the man complied.

A Spanish hospital, Vall d'Hebron in Barcelona, says it performed the world's most complex face transplant in February, a 27-hour operation involving 45 medical staff. The 45-year-old patient had suffered for 20 years from arteriovenous malformation, which deformed his face and impaired his vision and speech; the surgery reconstructed his lower face and neck, including his jaw, teeth, mouth, and tongue. Other hospitals had deemed him inoperable, but he has since recovered well, is living a normal life at home, and returns to the hospital only for routine check-ups.

King Felipe and Queen Letizia of Spain appeared together in public for the first time since a new book by journalist Ana Romero claimed that his father, former King Juan Carlos, had a decade-long affair with a German socialite and contemplated divorcing Queen Sofia. The couple kept composed at the Cervantes Prize ceremony, though the allegations are likely a blow to Felipe, who has worked to improve the monarchy's image by introducing a code of conduct banning lavish gifts and private business activity. Juan Carlos abdicated after a controversy over a costly Botswana hunting trip during Spain's

The tiny Aberdeenshire hamlet of Towie may sit on millions of pounds' worth of gold deposits, according to a two-year investigation by GreenOre, a Highland firm now backed by Turkish mining giant Koza Altin Isletmeleri. The companies are seeking planning permission for further drilling and testing, though GreenOre's managing director says the project is at a very early stage and that the exact location of any deposit is still unknown. Local streams have long yielded grains of gold, and the firm hopes to replicate the success of a 3.5 million ounce deposit being developed in Northern Ireland.

Korean carmaker SsangYong (meaning "two dragons") is launching its Tivoli sports utility vehicle in the UK this summer from under £13,000, pitched as a value-for-money rival to the Nissan Juke. It comes in SE, EX and ELX trim levels with 1.6 litre petrol and diesel engines, front-wheel drive or 4x4 options, seven airbags and a five-year unlimited mileage warranty. SsangYong's UK sales director expects the car to double the firm's annual UK sales from 2,000 to 4,000.

Liverpool winger Raheem Sterling, 20, was allegedly photographed smoking a shisha pipe in an image published by the Sunday Mirror, with a caption suggesting more smoking was planned that night. The incident comes shortly after he turned down a £100,000-a-week contract offer from Liverpool amid speculation he could leave the club this summer. Sterling is not the first England international caught with a shisha pipe: Arsenal's Jack Wilshere faced similar controversy in February, and manager Arsene Wenger criticized such behavior.

Elspeth McKendrick, a gifted 16-year-old prefect from Bury, hanged herself in August 2012, just weeks after earning a string of A* GCSE grades. An inquest heard she was depressed and "in denial" after being diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome the previous year, and felt unable to discuss it with anyone. She left a note apologising to her family and saying she wished she could open up to friends, despite having a small circle of friends and a place secured at Manchester College of Art.

The Direct Marketing Commission is formally investigating two firms exposed by the Daily Mail for selling private data: B2C Data, which sold financial details of 15,000 people, and Data Bubble, which supplied health information on 3,000 patients. Chief commissioner George Kidd called the allegations "serious," and both firms already face a probe by the Information Commissioner's Office over what it described as a very serious breach of the Data Protection Act. Undercover filming showed the firms' bosses boasting about the extensive data they held and selling it to the Mail's bogus cold-calling firm without carrying out any checks on it.

Authorities in New York and Connecticut are searching for a woman who stole the identity of Kate Sullivan, a 50-year-old fashion marketing executive, while she lay dying of lung cancer in a Manhattan hospital. Surveillance footage shows the suspect withdrawing $9,000 from Sullivan's Chase accounts on Long Island and then opening four store credit cards in New Haven, Connecticut, running up about $4,000 in bills. Sullivan died five days after learning of the fraud, and her sister has since had to deal with creditors and police while mourning, saying she wants to prevent others from going

As the trial of Auschwitz bookkeeper Oskar Groening draws global attention, the article highlights the former female SS guards who served at Nazi death camps and will likely escape justice. Of the 3,700 women who worked at the camps, only three were investigated by German prosecutors for complicity in mass murder, and all are now deemed too ill or infirm to be punished. One example is Charlotte S., a Ravensbrück and Auschwitz guard remembered by survivors for beating prisoners and setting her Alsatian dog on them, often with deadly results.

Janet and John Brennan bought the ruined 15th-century Barholm Castle in Dumfries and Galloway for £65,000 in 1997 and spent eight years and hundreds of thousands of pounds restoring it into a luxurious home. They have now put it on the market for offers over £695,000, a price that will leave them with a six-figure loss. Despite this, the couple call the project a "labour of love" and say they have "no regrets."

Sawyer Sweeten, the 19-year-old former child star of *Everybody Loves Raymond*, died by suicide on Thursday morning at a family member's home in Texas. His manager said the family is in "absolute shock," since Sweeten showed no signs of depression or other warning signs beforehand and was described as quiet, shy, and anti-drugs. Co-star Ray Romano said he was "terribly saddened," while Sweeten's sister Madylin asked for privacy and urged people to reach out to the ones they love.

Patrick Revins, 49, was caught selling £10 of heroin hidden in a Kinder Egg to an undercover police officer in November 2013, who easily identified him because he has the initials "P" and "R" tattooed on either side of his forehead. He admitted supplying heroin at Stoke-on-Trent Crown Court and was sentenced to a year in jail, to be added to the 27-month term he is already serving for knife possession. His distinctive tattoos also led to his arrest after he brandished a bread knife in a Staffordshire bank, while his co-defendant Nathan Davenport was jailed for 45

Authorities say 100-year-old Michael Juskin of New Jersey killed his 88-year-old wife, Rosalia, with an ax while she slept on Sunday night, then took his own life with a knife. A relative found the bodies Monday morning, and while the prosecutor said the couple had a "history of domestic issues," no motive has been determined. Neighbors and a relative said Michael had mental problems or dementia, and police confirmed they had visited the home a few times in recent years.

A study by the OECD, using Lisbon data in a computer model, found that shared self-driving "taxibots" could cut the number of cars needed for the same daily journeys by 90 per cent, or 77 per cent even with one passenger per ride and no complementary public transport. The authors added that replacing personal cars with these cabs would also free up parking space equal to over 200 football pitches in Lisbon. The findings come as firms like Google and Uber work on driverless taxi technology, though one trial coordinator warned that an accident involving a driverless car is inevitable.
